Hypothermia (very cold, shivering, confused or drowsy): get them indoors or to a sheltered place as quickly as possible, out of the wind and off the cold ground. Remove wet clothing and wrap them in dry blankets, a sleeping bag or towels, with the head covered. Handle them gently. If they're fully awake, give a warm non-alcoholic drink and something sugary like chocolate; give no drinks to someone who isn't fully awake. You can also warm them skin to skin under dry blankets. Don't use a hot bath, hot-water bottle, heat lamp or fire, don't rub their arms, legs, hands or feet, and don't give alcohol. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR and keep warming them. Call emergency services for anyone you think has hypothermia; don't drive them yourself if an ambulance can come.

Source: NHS, Hypothermia; St John Ambulance (UK), Hypothermia; CDC, Preventing Hypothermia. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

Head injury: if they might have hurt their neck (a fall from height, a high-speed hit) or aren't responding, don't move them unless they're in danger; support the head so the head, neck and spine stay in a straight line. If they're not responding and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR. If they're not responding but breathing normally, and they're vomiting or their breathing sounds blocked or gurgling, turn them on their side, keeping the head and spine in line. For a bump, hold an ice pack or frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel on it for short periods; never put ice directly on the skin. An adult should stay with them for the first 24 hours. They should rest, avoid alcohol until they feel better, and avoid contact sport for 3 weeks. Get urgent medical advice if they've been sick once, feel dizzy, take blood thinners, or had been drinking; if told to go to hospital, don't drive yourself. Call emergency services if they were knocked out and haven't woken, can't stay awake, have a seizure, vomit more than once, fell more than 1 metre or 5 stairs, were hit at high speed, have problems seeing, hearing, speaking, walking or with balance, new weakness or numbness, clear fluid from the ears or nose, bleeding from the ears, or changed behaviour.

Source: St John Ambulance (UK), Spinal injury; St John Ambulance (UK), Head injury; St John Ambulance (UK), CPR; British Heart Foundation, How to do CPR; St John Ambulance (UK), Recovery position; NHS, Head injury and concussion; British Red Cross, Head injury; healthdirect (AU), Head injuries. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.
